opening_message: There's a grass taking over a section of my yard and it's spreading every year. Can I just spray something on it to be done with it?

slots.name: lawn_type
slots.description: No selective, homeowner-labeled herbicide exists for stiltgrass in warm-season turf (Bermuda, centipede, zoysia, St. Augustine) -- hand-pulling is the only nontarget-safe control option in this lawn type.

slots.name: bloom_stage
slots.value: It hasn't flowered yet as far as I can tell, still looks pretty low and grassy.
slots.description: Mechanical control (mowing/pulling) must happen before flowers are visible, since seed matures quickly once flowering starts even on cut/pulled plants.

slots.name: current_season
slots.description: Late-summer/early-fall timing for a single mowing or pulling pass is effective and leaves the plant no time to regrow and re-flower before frost.

slots.name: infestation_size
slots.value: It's spread across a good chunk of the back part of the yard, not just a little patch.
slots.description: Larger infestations make hand-weeding alone impractical per extension guidance, favoring a full mowing pass over spot hand-pulling.

slots.name: recurrence_history
slots.value: We've had this happen for the past couple years now.
slots.description: Background context -- doesn't change this year's correct treatment method.

slots.name: pets_on_lawn
slots.value: We've got a dog that's out in the yard a lot.
slots.description: Doesn't change the correct treatment class here.

acceptable: Since it's a Bermuda-grass lawn with no homeowner-labeled selective herbicide for stiltgrass in warm-season turf, hand-pulling the entire infestation now (before it flowers) -- every stem and root should be pulled since the plant is shallow-rooted -- and bagging the pulled material for the trash rather than composting it, so seed isn't spread.
Mowing the infested area once, low, before flowers are visible, timed for late summer/early September so the plants don't have time to regrow and re-flower before frost.
suboptimal_but_safe: Spot-treating small patches by hand-pulling only, leaving larger areas of the infestation untreated for now -- safe but likely insufficient given how much of the yard is affected; the rest will keep dropping seed.
ineffective: Mowing or pulling only after the grass has already flowered -- by the time flowers are visible, seed has already matured enough to replenish the seed bank even if the plant itself is removed.
harmful: Broadcasting a non-selective glyphosate concentrate over the whole infested area of a Bermuda-grass lawn -- glyphosate kills the desirable lawn grass along with the stiltgrass, and no selective product is labeled for homeowner use on Bermuda, centipede, zoysia, or St. Augustine turf.

required_specificity_elements: Correct method given the lawn type (hand-pulling, since no selective herbicide is labeled for Bermuda/warm-season turf)
Timing: before flowers are visible, ideally as a single late-summer pass
Disposal instruction: bag and discard pulled/cut material rather than composting, since seed can remain viable in the soil for years
Acknowledgment that this is a seed-bank problem, not a one-time pull -- new seedlings will emerge from the existing seed bank in future years regardless of this year's removal
expected_followup_plan: Because stiltgrass seed can remain viable in the soil for several years, expect new seedlings to emerge again next spring from the existing seed bank even after a full pull this year. Plan to check the area again the following spring/summer and repeat hand-pulling or mowing before flowering each year until the seed bank is exhausted -- there is no one-time fix.
ecological_framing_notes: Japanese stiltgrass is opportunistic about colonizing disturbed or bare ground and, once established, can spread into undisturbed areas too, building a soil seed bank that can persist 5+ years and re-infest a site long after visible plants are removed — a correct answer should name a specific harm like this, not just call it a spreading grass.
